summary.en: Sucrose refined from cane or beet. Brown, raw, turbinado and 'evaporated cane juice' are the same molecule with a little molasses left in.

why.en: Added sugar. Its position in the list says how much: near the front means it's a main ingredient. Sage scores the sugar on the panel and the sweetener system, not the word on the label.

summary.en: Sap or fruit dried into crystals — marketed as unrefined, nutritionally almost pure sucrose.

why.en: Added sugar with a health halo. Trace minerals don't change how the body handles it.

summary.en: Starch broken down into sugars — a cheap, neutral-tasting sweetener and bulking agent.

why.en: Added sugar in syrup form; brown rice syrup is no exception. Counts fully toward the sugar Sage scores.

summary.en: Corn syrup with part of its glucose converted to fructose — close to table sugar in composition.

why.en: Added sugar. The evidence that HFCS is worse than sucrose at equal doses is thin; Sage treats it as sugar and flags it when it's on your avoid list.

summary.en: Glucose (dextrose) or short glucose chains (maltodextrin) made from starch — sweet, fast-absorbing, often used as filler.

why.en: Acts like sugar in the body even when the label's sugar line is low; Sage counts these as sugar and as isolate markers.

summary.en: The sugar that makes fruit sweet, isolated as a sweetener. Same effect as added sugar without the fruit's fiber.

why.en: Added sugar.

summary.en: Bee-made sugar syrup — mostly fructose and glucose, with trace enzymes and antioxidants.

why.en: Still added sugar: the trace compounds don't offset the sugar at the amounts used in food. Sage counts it as a whole-food ingredient but scores its sugar on the panel.

summary.en: Concentrated plant sap or juice — natural in origin, mostly sugar by weight.

why.en: Added sugar. Agave is especially high in fructose.

summary.en: Fruit juice with the water removed — a sweetener that lets the label read 'no added sugar'.

why.en: Functions as added sugar: the fiber is gone and the sugar is concentrated. Sage doesn't launder it.

summary.en: A chlorinated sugar derivative about 600× sweeter than sugar, not metabolized for energy.

why.en: Non-nutritive sweetener: safe at regulated levels, but part of a sweetener system Sage docks. Flagged when it's on your avoid list.

summary.en: A dipeptide sweetener ~200× sweeter than sugar. IARC lists it as 'possibly carcinogenic' (2B, limited evidence); regulators kept the ADI.

why.en: Non-nutritive sweetener. Sage docks sweetener systems and flags it on your avoid list; the 2B listing is about weak evidence, not proven harm.

summary.en: A potassium-salt sweetener, usually blended with sucralose or aspartame to round off the taste.

why.en: Non-nutritive sweetener in a blend — Sage docks the sweetener system as a whole.

summary.en: The oldest artificial sweetener. The 1970s bladder-cancer scare was rat-specific and was withdrawn.

why.en: Non-nutritive sweetener; part of the sweetener system Sage docks.

summary.en: Sweet glycosides extracted and purified from the stevia leaf, ~300× sweeter than sugar.

why.en: Plant-derived, but still a high-intensity sweetener: it keeps the palate tuned to sweet. Sage docks it lighter than a multi-sweetener system.

summary.en: Mogrosides extracted from the luo han guo fruit; usually blended with erythritol for bulk.

why.en: High-intensity sweetener; check the blend — the erythritol that usually rides along is the bulk of the 'monk fruit' in the jar.

summary.en: Sugar alcohols: bulk sweeteners with fewer calories. Maltitol and sorbitol are laxative above ~20–30 g; xylitol is toxic to dogs.

why.en: Counted in the sweetener system and, when declared, as polyol load. A 'sugar-free' bar can carry 15 g of these.

summary.en: Oil pressed from olives without heat or solvents; rich in oleic acid and polyphenols.

why.en: Sage's top fat tier — minimally refined, with the strongest human evidence of any culinary fat.

summary.en: Pressed from the fruit or nut. Mostly monounsaturated (avocado, macadamia) or omega-3 rich (flax, walnut, hemp).

why.en: Top fat tier when cold-pressed; refined versions lose some of the case.

summary.en: Dairy fat — butter, ghee or cream. Mostly saturated fat, a little short-chain fatty acid.

why.en: Fine as an ingredient: it's real food. Its saturated fat is judged on the nutrition panel, not here.

summary.en: Plant fats that are solid at room temperature — coconut, cocoa, shea. High in saturated fat; cocoa butter is the fat in real chocolate.

why.en: Fine as an ingredient. Saturated fat is scored on the panel; Sage doesn't buy the 'superfood' framing either way.

summary.en: Refined, semi-solid tropical oil — the cheap structural fat in spreads, biscuits and bars. Heavily refined and deodorized.

why.en: Low fat-quality tier: high in palmitic saturated fat and refined hard. The environmental record isn't scored — only the health side is.

summary.en: Oils extracted from seeds with heat and solvent, then refined, bleached and deodorized. Mostly polyunsaturated (omega-6) or, for canola and high-oleic versions, monounsaturated.

why.en: Low fat tier. The omega-6 'inflammation' claim is weak in human trials; Sage docks these for the refining and the missing polyphenols — not as toxins. They're flagged when seed oils are on your avoid list.

summary.en: An unspecified refined oil — in practice palm, soybean or rapeseed blends.

why.en: Low fat tier: refined, and the source isn't even declared. Sage can't give credit for an oil it can't identify.

summary.en: Oil hardened by forcing in hydrogen. Partial hydrogenation creates industrial trans fat; full hydrogenation and interesterification avoid it but produce hard, highly engineered fats.

why.en: Avoid: the trans-fat family has no safe intake, and Sage caps the overall score when trans fat shows on the panel. Even the trans-free versions sit in the lowest fat tier.

summary.en: Rendered animal fat — mostly monounsaturated and saturated, with no refining beyond melting.

why.en: Fine as an ingredient; saturated fat is judged on the panel.

summary.en: Flour milled from the entire kernel — bran, germ and endosperm — so the fiber and micronutrients stay in.

why.en: A whole grain. Sage's graded whole-grain rule credits it by position in the list, not by the claim on the front.

summary.en: The whole oat kernel, rolled or milled. Naturally high in beta-glucan fiber.

why.en: A whole grain — counts toward Sage's real-food ratio and its whole-grain credit.

summary.en: Intact or minimally milled grains and seeds with their bran and germ.

why.en: Whole food and whole grain — credited in the real-food ratio and, where the profile scores it, the whole-grain rule.

summary.en: Flour or grain with the bran and germ removed. 'Enriched' means a few B vitamins and iron were added back; the fiber wasn't.

why.en: Fine — a staple, not a hazard. It just isn't a whole grain, so it earns no whole-grain credit and contributes little fiber.

summary.en: Purified starch — a thickener and bulking agent. 'Modified' means treated to hold up under heat, acid or freezing.

why.en: Fine on its own; it's a processing marker Sage uses to recognize formulation, not an ingredient it docks.

summary.en: Fluid milk or a traditional dairy food made from it.

why.en: A whole food — counts toward Sage's real-food ratio. Fat and sodium are judged on the panel.

summary.en: Milk with the water removed, or a fraction of it (whey, casein). Common in chocolate spreads, bars and baked goods.

why.en: Fine — a dairy ingredient, not a concern on its own. Sage treats milk and whey powders as whole-food-derived, not as isolates.

summary.en: Protein separated from milk, soy, peas or rice for protein bars, powders and shakes. Collagen is an incomplete protein (low in tryptophan).

why.en: Fine: isolates are how a protein bar delivers protein, and Sage's protein-bar profile never docks them. Source quality is scored — collagen earns far less than whey or egg.

summary.en: Whole egg, white or yolk — fresh, liquid or dried.

why.en: A whole food; high-quality complete protein. Counts toward Sage's real-food ratio.

summary.en: Tree nuts, peanuts or a butter ground from them.

why.en: Whole food — fiber, unsaturated fat and protein. Counts toward the real-food ratio; hero-ingredient rules check whether it's actually there in quantity.

summary.en: Whole or ground seeds.

why.en: Whole food — counts toward Sage's real-food ratio.

summary.en: The ground cocoa bean or its defatted powder. Alkalizing ('Dutch process') mellows the flavor and reduces flavanols somewhat.

why.en: Whole food — flavanol-rich. Counts toward the real-food ratio; the sugar that usually travels with it is scored separately.

summary.en: A sub-recipe of cocoa, sugar and fat. 'Compound' or 'chocolatey coating' swaps cocoa butter for palm or other vegetable fat.

why.en: Neutral as a whole; look at what's in the parentheses — the sugar and fat inside it are what Sage actually scores.

summary.en: Fruit with the water removed — fiber and micronutrients intact, sugar concentrated.

why.en: Whole food, and Sage credits it as such. But it is sugar-dense: a date bar can carry 30 g of sugar per 100 g, and the fruit-sugar discount is capped so that can't hide entirely.

summary.en: Fruit, vegetables or legumes — fresh, frozen, puréed or cooked.

why.en: Whole food — counts toward the real-food ratio and the fruit/vegetable/nut share.

summary.en: Sodium chloride — sea, rock or mined, iodized or not. Nutritionally identical.

why.en: Fine as an ingredient: how much sodium ends up in the food is judged on the panel, not by the word 'salt'.

summary.en: Water.

why.en: Not judged, and left out of Sage's real-food ratio so it can't pad a short list.

summary.en: A proprietary mix of flavor compounds. 'Natural' means the starting material was plant or animal; the processing can be extensive and the recipe is never disclosed.

why.en: Fine on its own — no evidence of harm at food-use levels. Sage uses flavorings as one marker of ultra-processing, not as a dock by itself.

summary.en: A stimulant, added or from guarana / coffee / tea extracts. Taurine is an amino acid common in energy drinks, not a stimulant itself.

why.en: Neutral at typical amounts; Sage shows the milligrams in the Detected section and the drinks profile caps heavily caffeinated products.

summary.en: Acids used for preservation, tang and pH control — vinegar, citrus juice or citric acid (which is fermented from sugar, not squeezed from lemons).

why.en: Fine. Traditional preservation; citric acid (E330) is a low-risk additive.

summary.en: Leavening or fermentation agents — yeast, sourdough culture, baking soda / powder, or the live cultures and enzymes in dairy.

why.en: Fine — traditional food processing, not a formulation trick. No effect on the score by itself.

summary.en: Dried herbs and spices, alone or as a blend.

why.en: Fine — flavor from real plants. 'Seasoning' and 'spices' can hide salt, but that shows up on the sodium line.

summary.en: A fatty emulsifier extracted from soybeans or sunflower seeds (E322); it keeps chocolate smooth and fat from separating.

why.en: Fine: low-risk additive at food levels. It is still an emulsifier, so it counts as a processing marker — not a dock on its own.

summary.en: Fiber isolated from chicory, corn or oats and added back to lift the fiber line. Inulin and IMO can cause bloating in larger doses.

why.en: Fine, with a caveat: Sage counts isolated fiber at half weight on bars and refined-grain breads, because a fiber line inflated this way doesn't behave like the fiber in whole grains.

summary.en: Thickeners and stabilizers — plant gums, seaweed extracts (carrageenan, agar), pectin or gelatin.

why.en: Fine at food levels; carrageenan is on some avoid lists for gut-irritation evidence that is mostly from animal and cell studies. Sage flags it when it's on yours.

summary.en: A preservative — chemical (sorbate, benzoate, propionate), curing (nitrite / nitrate, including 'cultured celery' which is nitrite by another route) or antioxidant (ascorbate, tocopherols, rosemary).

why.en: Most are fine at food levels; Sage rates each in the Additives section by its own evidence. Nitrite-cured meat is the exception worth limiting — the additive rating says so.

match: fruit and vegetable juice for color

summary.en: A colorant — plant-derived (beet, paprika, annatto, turmeric, spirulina), insect-derived (carmine) or a class-IV caramel.

why.en: Plant colors are fine. Synthetic dyes and ammonia caramels are rated individually in the Additives section and flagged if artificial colors are on your avoid list.

summary.en: Soy in a processed form — flour, milk, textured protein or fermented (miso, tamari, tempeh).

why.en: Fine: a legitimate protein source. Tofu, tempeh and edamame count as whole foods; the textured and isolated forms are neutral processed ingredients.

summary.en: A plant 'milk' — a small share of oat, almond, pea or rice blended into water, usually with added oil, salt and fortification.

why.en: Neutral: what matters is the rest of the list (oil, sugar, gums) and the fortification. The name promises more nut or grain than the recipe usually contains.

summary.en: Wheat protein concentrated from flour; lifts bread dough and doesn't behave like an isolate sweetener.

why.en: Fine — Sage's bread profile deliberately doesn't treat it as an ultra-processing marker.

summary.en: Fortification — vitamins and minerals added to the food, or (potassium / sodium citrate, calcium phosphate) acidity and mineral salts.

why.en: Fine. Sage exempts fortification from the additive and processing docks — vitamin D in milk or iron in flour isn't a formulation trick.

summary.en: Ethanol, as an ingredient or carrier.

why.en: Worth limiting: no level of alcohol is neutral for health, though the trace amounts in extracts and flavorings don't matter.
